question: What is the primary objective of commercial accounting in a business entity?
options: To calculate government taxes only
To systematically record, classify, summarize, and report financial performance and position
To print bills for retail customers
To track daily employee attendance
explanation: Accounting systematically records transactions in journals, posts to ledgers, and prepares financial reports (P&L and Balance Sheet) to evaluate profitability and financial health.

question: According to the Business Entity Concept, how is the owner's capital treated in accounting?
options: As a personal expense of the owner
As a liability of the business towards the proprietor
As an operating asset of the firm
As a bank revenue gain
explanation: The Business Entity Concept treats the business as separate from its owner. Capital introduced by the owner is an internal liability owed by the business back to the owner.

question: If a business has Total Assets of ₹15,00,000 and External Liabilities of ₹6,00,000, what is the Owner's Capital?
explanation: According to the Accounting Equation: Capital = Total Assets (₹15,00,000) - External Liabilities (₹6,00,000) = ₹9,00,000.

question: Under traditional classification of accounts, under which category does 'Cash in Hand' belong?
options: Personal Account
Nominal Account
Real Account
Representative Personal Account
explanation: Real Accounts represent tangible or intangible properties and assets owned by the business entity, such as Cash, Building, Machinery, and Stock.

question: What is the Golden Rule of Accounting for Nominal Accounts?
options: Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out
Debit the receiver, Credit the giver
Debit all expenses & losses, Credit all incomes & gains
Debit all assets, Credit all liabilities
explanation: Nominal Accounts (expenses, losses, revenues, gains) follow the rule: Debit all expenses & losses, Credit all incomes & gains.

question: Under modern debit-credit rules, what happens when an Asset Account increases?
options: It is Credited (+)
It is Debited (+)
It remains unchanged
It is converted into a liability
explanation: Under modern classification, Asset and Expense accounts carry normal debit balances. An increase in an asset is DEBITED and a decrease is CREDITED.

question: How is a routine repair expense of ₹5,000 to maintain office machinery classified?
options: Capital Expenditure (added to Machinery Asset)
Revenue Expenditure (debited to Repair & Maintenance Expense)
Deferred Revenue Expenditure
Personal drawings of the proprietor
explanation: Routine maintenance costs preserve existing operational efficiency without increasing long-term capacity; thus it is a Revenue Expenditure debited to P&L.

question: When a firm pays ₹25,000 cash for shop rent, what accounts are debited and credited?
options: Debit Cash A/c, Credit Rent A/c
Debit Rent A/c (Nominal Expense), Credit Cash A/c (Real Asset -)
Debit Rent A/c, Credit Landlord Personal A/c
Debit Capital A/c, Credit Cash A/c
explanation: Rent is a nominal operating expense (Debit all expenses); Cash is a real asset leaving the firm (Credit what goes out).

question: When goods costing ₹50,000 are purchased on credit from vendor 'Bengal Electricals', what is the entry in TallyPrime F9 Purchase Voucher?
options: Debit Purchase A/c ₹50,000; Credit Bengal Electricals (Sundry Creditor) A/c ₹50,000
Debit Cash A/c ₹50,000; Credit Purchase A/c ₹50,000
Debit Bengal Electricals A/c ₹50,000; Credit Sales A/c ₹50,000
Debit Capital A/c ₹50,000; Credit Bank A/c ₹50,000
explanation: Purchasing inventory on credit increases Purchase expense (Debit Purchase) and creates a vendor trade liability (Credit Sundry Creditor Bengal Electricals).

question: Which TallyPrime voucher type is used to record non-cash adjusting entries, depreciation, and bad debt write-offs?
options: F4 Contra Voucher
F5 Payment Voucher
F6 Receipt Voucher
F7 Journal Voucher
explanation: F7 Journal Voucher in TallyPrime is dedicated to non-cash book adjustments, depreciation, bad debt write-offs, and period closing entries.
